title: Iraq's New Premier Vows to Disarm Iran-Backed Militias as a Trump-Xi Summit Looms Over a $14 Billion Taiwan Arms Sale
subhead: Ali al-Zaidi pledged to dismantle the militias that underpin Iranian influence in Iraq, while Beijing presses Washington to freeze a Taiwan weapons sale ahead of Xi's visit. Separately, the Houthis bombed Riyadh, and Typhoon Dujuan hammered Japan.

sections.heading: Iraq's Premier Takes On the Iran-Backed Militias
sections.body:
Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, a political newcomer, has vowed to disarm the Iran-backed militias that have given Tehran a dominant lever inside Iraq for two decades, according to an interview reported by The New York Times. Al-Zaidi laid out an ambitious timeline, staking his credibility on a task that has defeated every previous Iraqi leader who attempted it.

The pledge matters well beyond Baghdad. Iranian-backed factions, many of them part of the Popular Mobilization Forces, have been a key conduit for Tehran's regional strategy, launching drone and rocket attacks and providing a rear base for pressure campaigns. A credible disarmament drive would not only reshape Iraq's internal balance of power but also directly loosen Iran's grip on a strategic neighbor that borders both Saudi Arabia and Syria.
sections.whyItMatters: If al-Zaidi follows through, Iran loses its most reliable proxy infrastructure on its western flank — a geopolitical shift as significant as any battlefield outcome in the broader war.

sections.heading: Trump and Xi Prepare for a Summit Shadowed by Taiwan Arms
sections.body:
Ahead of Xi Jinping's visit to Washington next week, Beijing is pressing President Trump to freeze a proposed $14 billion weapons sale to Taiwan, The New York Times reports. Taiwan, in turn, is trying to demonstrate that its security remains in American interests. Xi appears to want to lock in a tactical truce with an American president constrained by the Iran war and domestic politics, even as the two powers hold talks on an AI safety plan, per the BBC.

Japan's prime minister is also set to meet Trump to seek help balancing China's economic and security pressure while trying to de-escalate with Beijing. The cluster of meetings means the shape of US-China relations for the next year may be decided in a single week of summits.
sections.whyItMatters: The Taiwan arms sale is the single most likely flashpoint to blow up the fragile US-China truce, and this week's summit will reveal whether Xi gets his freeze or Washington holds the line.

sections.heading: Houthis Bomb Riyadh as the Yemen War Opens a Second Front
sections.body:
In what The New York Times calls a significant escalation, Iran-backed Houthi forces fired a wave of ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi capital Riyadh and at Saudi oil facilities, alongside fierce ground battles with Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. The Houthis are pushing to expand territory in Yemen, and civilians are fleeing across the Red Sea to Djibouti, per the BBC.

Al Jazeera reports that the United Kingdom has agreed to refuel Saudi jets to help counter the Houthi attacks — a concrete Western commitment to the Saudi war effort. The NYT characterizes the conflict as a second Middle East front that opened after the United States and Israel attacked Iran, adding to energy-market turmoil.
sections.whyItMatters: A confirmed missile-and-drone attack on Riyadh and a UK pledge to refuel Saudi aircraft pull the West and Gulf states deeper into a parallel war that directly threatens energy infrastructure and the Bab al-Mandab shipping route.

sections.heading: Typhoon Dujuan Slams Japan, Disrupting the Region
sections.body:
A powerful Typhoon Dujuan struck Japan, killing at least two people and causing travel chaos around Tokyo, with millions urged to evacuate, according to Al Jazeera and the BBC. The storm forced airport and rail shutdowns and tested disaster-response systems in the world's third-largest economy.

Beyond the human toll, the disruption hits at a sensitive moment: Japan's prime minister is heading into meetings with President Trump over China strategy, and any extended infrastructure or supply-chain fallout from the typhoon could complicate both domestic recovery and the diplomatic week ahead.
sections.whyItMatters: Typhoon recovery costs and any prolonged energy or logistics disruption could weigh on Japan just as it seeks leverage with Washington and Beijing.

sections.heading: Putin Consolidates Control in a Choreographed Election
sections.body:
Russia's governing party won a supermajority in a parliamentary election that Western news outlets, including The New York Times and Al Jazeera, characterize as engineered to project that Putin remains firmly in control. The result was widely expected and largely unchanged in substance, but the timing matters: it locks in an unambiguous political posture at home while Moscow continues its drone campaign that saw hundreds of drones target Moscow on the final day of voting, per the NYT.

Russia also warned that the new US sanctions law would harm Trump's peace efforts, signaling that the Kremlin sees the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict as interconnected bargaining fronts.
sections.whyItMatters: A consolidated Russian political position removes any internal check on Putin's negotiating stance just as the US-China summit and Middle East diplomacy converge on the same week.

bottomLine: Today's strategic picture is defined by converging summit diplomacy and a spreading Middle East conflict. Iraq's new premier is attempting the boldest rollback of Iranian influence in Baghdad in two decades, while the Trump-Xi meeting over Taiwan arms will set the tone for great-power competition. In parallel, the Houthis' strike on Riyadh — now answered with UK commitments to refuel Saudi jets — turns Yemen into a second, energy-threatening front. The week ahead, not the day's headlines, will decide whether any of these threads resolve or intensify.
